name: Battle of Evesham (1265)
eventLocation: Green Hill, north of Evesham, with the town in a loop of the River Avon behind

imageInfo.caption: Simon de Montfort cut down at Evesham, in a colour wood engraving printed by Edmund Evans for James Doyle’s A Chronicle of England, 1864.
imageInfo.creator: James William Edmund Doyle, colour-printed by Edmund Evans
imageInfo.note: A Victorian reconstruction, not evidence: no depiction of the battle made at the time survives beyond a few chronicle drawings. Doyle put Montfort in the centre with the forked red lion of his arms on his surcoat, horse down, surrounded; the red crosses on the attackers are the badge the royal army wore that day. The detail is nineteenth-century antiquarian guesswork, but the essentials - Montfort dismounted, encircled and killed rather than taken for ransom - follow the chronicle accounts. Public domain.

sectionImages.note: The nearest thing to contemporary evidence for what was done to the body, drawn within a generation of the battle. Montfort is shown with his head, hands and feet struck off, identified by the forked lion on the shield beside him; Hugh Despenser, killed in the same encirclement, lies above with the Despenser arms on his surcoat. Public domain.

summary: The Lord Edward trapped Simon de Montfort in a loop of the Avon at Evesham on 4 August 1265 and destroyed his army in a thunderstorm, killing him and mutilating his body, and with him the baronial revolt.
details: Fifteen months after his victory at Lewes, Montfort was caught between a river and an army three times his size. Edward blocked the only bridge, came on under banners captured from Montfort’s son two days earlier, and gave no quarter: a squad was detailed to find the earl and kill him. The war dragged on for two more years at Kenilworth and Ely, but it was decided here.
outcome: Decisive royalist victory. Simon de Montfort, his son Henry, Hugh Despenser and Peter de Montfort were killed, Henry III was freed, and baronial government ended.

contentSections.title: Overview
paragraphs: On the morning of 4 August 1265 the Lord Edward caught Simon de Montfort at Evesham, in a loop of the River Avon with the only bridge held against him, and destroyed his army in about two hours under a summer thunderstorm. Montfort was killed and his body cut apart on the field. His son Henry de Montfort, Hugh Despenser the justiciar and Peter de Montfort died with him, and the baronial regime that had governed England since the Battle of Lewes ended with them.

Contemporaries did not think it was a battle in the ordinary sense. Robert of Gloucester called it "the murder of Evesham, for battle it was none", and the phrase has stuck because it is accurate: the royalists refused the usual convention of taking noble prisoners for ransom, and set men aside specifically to kill Montfort rather than capture him. Henry III himself, held in Montfort’s line and dressed in Montfort’s colours, was wounded and nearly cut down by his own son’s men before he could shout who he was.

contentSections.title: Background: from Lewes to the Severn
paragraphs: Montfort had ruled England in Henry’s name since May 1264, through a council of nine and with the king and the Lord Edward as hostages. The base of that rule narrowed steadily. Gilbert de Clare, Earl of Gloucester, who had commanded the baronial centre at Lewes, fell out with him over castles, offices and the share of the spoils taken by Montfort’s own sons, and went over to the royalists in the spring of 1265.

On 28 May 1265 Edward escaped from loose custody at Hereford, reportedly by trying out horses until his guards’ mounts were blown, and joined Gloucester and Roger Mortimer in the Marches. He took Gloucester town on 29 June, which closed the Severn crossings, and Montfort found himself pinned in south Wales. Montfort bought Welsh support at a heavy price in the treaty he made with Llywelyn ap Gruffudd in June, conceding lands and recognition that no English government would have granted from strength.

The last act was a race for a junction. Montfort recrossed the Severn at Kempsey on 2 August, heading to meet the army his son Simon the Younger was bringing from the east. Edward got to the younger Simon first: on the night of 1 August he surprised his camp outside Kenilworth, scattered the force and took its banners. Montfort reached Evesham late on 3 August with an army that was never going to be reinforced, and halted there to let his men eat and hear mass.

contentSections.title: The trap and the ground
paragraphs: Evesham sits inside a tight loop of the Avon, entered from the north and left by a single bridge to the south-east. It is an excellent place to rest an army and a very bad place to be found in. Edward came down from the north and put his three divisions across the neck of the loop on the rising ground called Green Hill, under his own command, Gloucester’s and Mortimer’s, while Mortimer’s men also took the bridge behind the town. There was no line of retreat left.

Edward then used the banners taken at Kenilworth. Montfort’s watchman, sent up the abbey bell tower, first reported friendly colours approaching and only afterwards, as the columns closed, the royal arms behind them. By the time the deception was seen through, the divisions were deployed across the only way out. The chronicle tradition gives Montfort a soldier’s compliment on seeing the array - that they had learnt that order from him - and the grim remark that their souls were God’s and their bodies the enemy’s; both are set-pieces written after the fact, but they capture what the ground plainly showed.

The royal army was the larger by a wide margin. The Battlefields Trust puts the advantage at about three to one and the rebel army at possibly six thousand at most, which is as far as the evidence reasonably goes; the round ten thousand against five thousand quoted in popular accounts is that ratio dressed up as a count. Montfort’s force was also unbalanced: a core of knights, and a body of Welsh infantry supplied by Llywelyn that deserted early and was cut down in the cornfields and the river.

contentSections.title: The battle
paragraphs: Montfort marched out of the town some time after eight in the morning and attacked rather than waited, concentrating his knights into a wedge aimed at the centre of the royal line, hoping to punch through it and break out northwards. The weather turned as he moved: a thunderstorm blackened the sky, and several chroniclers record the darkness, the rain and the thunder as the fighting opened, which is why the storm is part of every telling of Evesham.

The wedge drove the royal centre back and then stopped. Gloucester’s and Mortimer’s divisions closed in on both flanks, and the baronial force was encircled on open ground with a river at its back. The Welsh foot had already gone. What followed was less a battle than a killing: the royalists had agreed beforehand to take no ransoms from the leaders, and pressed until the ring collapsed. The fighting ran back through the streets of Evesham and, the sources say, into the abbey itself, where men were cut down at the altars.

Henry de Montfort was killed early. Hugh Despenser, Peter de Montfort and Ralph Basset died in the encirclement; Guy de Montfort was badly wounded and taken. Henry III, whom Montfort had brought onto the field in armour and Montfort’s own colours, was struck and wounded in the press and saved only by crying out that he was Henry of Winchester, their king - Roger de Leybourne, a former rebel now back in the royal peace, got him clear. Royal losses were slight. Rebel losses were heavy, though the figures of seven and a half to ten thousand that appear in the record are rejected as improbable by the Battlefields Trust’s own assessment of the battlefield.

contentSections.title: The killing of Simon de Montfort
paragraphs: A squad of about a dozen men had been detailed to find Montfort and kill him, which is the clearest evidence that this was intended as an execution rather than a defeat. He lost his horse and fought on foot until he was brought down; one strand of the tradition has Roger Mortimer put a lance through his neck. What was done afterwards was deliberate and public: the head, hands, feet and genitals were cut from the body, and the head was sent to Wigmore Castle as a present for Mortimer’s wife, Maud de Braose.

The mutilation was a political statement about a man the royalists regarded as a traitor and a foreigner who had imprisoned his king, and it misfired. The monks of Evesham gathered what was left of the trunk and buried it before the high altar of the abbey, and within months pilgrims were reporting miracles at the grave and at the spring by the battlefield. An unofficial cult of Simon de Montfort as a martyr grew up across the Midlands, was fed by the songs and verses the reform party had already produced, and was suppressed with some difficulty by a crown that had to forbid the veneration of a rebel.

The abbey was pulled down at the Dissolution and the grave lost; the site is marked today near the surviving bell tower. The drawing in Cotton MS Nero D ii, made within a generation of the battle, is the closest thing to a contemporary record of what was done to the body, and it shows the dismemberment plainly enough that no later account had to invent it.

contentSections.title: Aftermath: the Dictum of Kenilworth
paragraphs: The immediate settlement was punitive. A parliament at Winchester in September 1265 declared the rebels disinherited outright, which turned survivors with nothing left to lose into a guerrilla problem. Resistance went on for two years: the younger Simon’s rising in Lincolnshire lasted to Christmas 1265, a garrison held the almost unassailable Kenilworth Castle through a siege that began on 21 June 1266 and only surrendered to hunger and disease on 14 December, and a band held the Isle of Ely into 1267.

The way out was the Dictum of Kenilworth, published on 31 October 1266 and drafted by a committee of bishops, earls and barons. It reversed the blanket disinheritance and put a price on returning to the king’s peace instead: most rebels could buy their lands back for five times the annual value, the heavily committed - Robert Ferrers, Earl of Derby, and Henry de Hastings who commanded at Kenilworth - paid seven, those who had merely incited paid two years’ value, and minor participants one. The terms were eased in 1267 after Gloucester, once again out of patience with the government, occupied London to press the point.

The Statute of Marlborough of November 1267 closed the war by writing the workable parts of the reform into law in the crown’s own name, confirming Magna Carta and much of the legal substance of the Provisions of Oxford while abandoning the baronial council that had enforced them. Henry III reigned quietly until 1272. Edward, who had settled the kingdom in a morning at Evesham, was on crusade when his father died and came home two years later to an untroubled succession - the first time since 1066 that the English crown changed hands with the heir abroad and nobody in arms.

strength.note: The Battlefields Trust gives possibly up to about 6,000 and rejects the recorded rebel casualty figures of 7,500–10,000 as improbable. Montfort was outnumbered and knew it before he attacked.

leaders.name: Simon de Montfort, Earl of Leicester
leaders.note: No biography in the Codex yet: leader of the reform party and ruler of England since Lewes, killed and mutilated here.

leaders.name: Henry de Montfort
leaders.note: No biography in the Codex yet: Simon’s eldest son, who had commanded on the baronial right at Lewes and was killed early in this battle.

battleContinuity.label: Edward's war-making goes north
battleContinuity.reason: Evesham made the Lord Edward’s reputation and handed him a settled kingdom to inherit in 1272. The army and the methods he built on it conquered Wales and then went into Scotland, where in 1297 William Wallace and Andrew Moray destroyed an English army at Stirling Bridge.

timeline.title: Montfort wins at Lewes
timeline.description: The king, his brother and his heir are captured, and Montfort governs England through a council of nine.

timeline.title: Gloucester changes sides
timeline.description: Gilbert de Clare quarrels with Montfort over castles and spoils and joins the royalists in the Marches.

timeline.title: Edward escapes from Hereford
timeline.description: The hostage taken at Lewes gets away and raises an army with Gloucester and Roger Mortimer.

timeline.title: Gloucester town taken
timeline.description: Edward closes the Severn crossings, pinning Montfort in south Wales.

timeline.title: The younger Simon surprised
timeline.description: Edward scatters Simon de Montfort the Younger’s camp outside Kenilworth and captures his banners.

timeline.title: Montfort recrosses the Severn
timeline.description: He fords at Kempsey, marching to join a son whose army has already been broken.

timeline.title: The battle
timeline.description: Edward blocks the loop of the Avon under the captured banners; Montfort is encircled, killed and dismembered in a thunderstorm.

timeline.title: The rebels disinherited
timeline.description: A parliament at Winchester strips the rebels of their lands outright, prolonging the resistance.

timeline.title: Dictum of Kenilworth
timeline.description: Rebels may buy their lands back at five times the annual value, or seven for the most deeply committed.

timeline.title: Kenilworth surrenders
timeline.description: The garrison holds out through a six-month siege and gives in to hunger and disease.

timeline.title: Statute of Marlborough
timeline.description: Much of the reform programme becomes law in the crown’s own name, and the war ends.
